title: Retirement savings: 'Quite a different tax bill' for same super returns
full_text:
Wealthy members of big industry and retail superannuation funds could face different bills for very similar investment returns under the Albanese government's tax on super balances above $3 million, creating fresh concerns about the effects of the contentious new levy.
Two months after the law came into force, super funds are still grappling with how to assess the investment returns to determine tax obligations for high-balance members because the legislation allows broad interpretations of how much is owed.
The law said earnings in superannuation funds such as AustralianSuper, Australian Retirement Trust and Hostplus must be allocated to members on a "fair and reasonable" basis. Funds must consider factors such as earnings, changes in asset values, the investment options invested in and if a member switched options, such as from high-growth to balanced, during the year.
A super industry participant involved in private discussions said funds were trying to figure out how to calculate the earnings so the tax was applied as consistently as possible.
"For the industry and retail funds there are still lots of issues to work out," they said, speaking on the condition of anonymity. "Investors in different super funds might get quite a different tax bill for the same investment and very similar circumstances."
The government in March passed legislation to double the tax rate to 30 per cent on earnings from super balances above $3 million. Returns from balances above $10 million face a total tax rate of up to 40 per cent.
The tax, which took effect on July 1, attracted fierce criticism when first announced by the government, which framed the change as a vital measure to rein in multimillion-dollar tax-sheltered accounts and pay for superannuation top-ups for low-income earners.
The measure was forecast to raise more than $2 billion in extra revenue a year.
Chalmers in March backed down on his original plan, which would have taxed unrealised capital gains on super balances above $3 million and was not indexed to inflation.
While the super industry generally welcomed the modification, taxing only realised gains was much harder for large industry and retail super funds to implement.
There was still time to work through the dilemma, with the tax bills due to be issued by the Australian Taxation Office in the second half of next year.
About 90,000 people, or less than 0.5 per cent of the population, have more than $3 million in super, the vast majority of whom have self-managed funds.
Typically, only hundreds of people at each of the big super funds have balances over the threshold, sometimes through combinations of their holdings in major funds and SMSFs.
Hostplus chief executive David Elia said only a small proportion of its members would be affected given the demographic profile of the fund, which included many workers in hospitality, tourism, recreation and sports.
"The key challenge is developing a robust and consistent methodology for attributing earnings to individual members in a way that appropriately reflects their underlying investment interests," he said.
"Hostplus is working through the implementation requirements and developing an attribution methodology in accordance with the legislative framework and any supporting guidance.
"We are engaging with our tax advisers, service providers and industry as part of that process, with a focus on ensuring outcomes appropriately reflect members' underlying investment interests."
Industry fund giants AustralianSuper and Australian Retirement Trust declined to comment.
Another source from a major super fund, who requested anonymity to speak freely, said there were challenges around calculating earnings for unlisted assets that had not been sold and how frequently to calculate members switching between investment options.
"You could potentially end up with different outcomes depending on what methodology you're using and back-end tech systems to calculate it," they said.
Most big super funds were not keen to publicly highlight the imprecise way investment returns would be allocated and tax calculated for members with total balances above $3 million.
The industry lobbied for a flexible approach to attribute earnings to avoid building major new IT and accounting systems that would cost millions of dollars for members, the vast majority of whom would not pay the extra tax.
Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia chief executive Mary Delahunty downplayed the issue and said super funds already attributed investment earnings to members through unit pricing and return attributions across their various investment options.
"Trustees must comply with a comprehensive framework of duties, including acting with care, skill and diligence, treating members fairly and acting in the best financial interests of the members as a whole," she said.
"Any approach to attribution will be consistent with those obligations. It is not uncommon for a legal duty to be principles-based and non-prescriptive.
"We expect the ATO to provide guidance on attribution for division 296 purposes, with fund processes being subject to the ATO's review. Differences might arise between investment options, earnings and the timing of realised gains between funds."
A spokeswoman for the ATO said it was developing guidance on what the law required on attribution.
In response to an inquiry to Chalmers, a Treasury spokesman said the legislation and regulations were intended to guide funds in attributing earnings to members on a fair and reasonable basis.
